title: Chapter 12 Drill: Peri-Operative Care, Surgical Procedures, and Complications

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman becomes hypotensive and tachycardic shortly after insertion of the primary trocar for laparoscopic cystectomy. The abdomen is not distended and no blood is seen in the field, but the camera shows a retroperitoneal bulge over the sacral promontory. What is the best next step?
options: Convert to laparotomy with vascular surgery assistance
Continue laparoscopy and observe the hematoma
Increase insufflation pressure to tamponade the bleeding
Give fluids and complete the cystectomy before evaluation
items.explanation: Hypotension with an expanding retroperitoneal hematoma after trocar entry suggests injury to the aorta, iliac vessels, or vena cava, which is a surgical emergency. Prompt laparotomy with vascular expertise and resuscitation is required. Watching the hematoma allows exsanguination. Higher insufflation pressure raises embolism risk and does not control a major vessel. Completing the planned procedure delays lifesaving repair.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with a penicillin allergy characterized by anaphylaxis is scheduled for abdominal hysterectomy. Which prophylactic regimen is appropriate?
options: Cefazolin 2 g intravenously
Clindamycin plus gentamicin
Ampicillin plus sulbactam
Oral amoxicillin the evening before surgery
items.explanation: A history of anaphylaxis to penicillin makes beta-lactam agents unsafe, so clindamycin combined with an aminoglycoside such as gentamicin provides coverage against skin flora and vaginal organisms. Cefazolin carries a small cross-reactivity risk and is avoided after immediate-type reactions. Ampicillin with sulbactam is itself a penicillin. A preoperative oral dose does not give adequate tissue levels at incision.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has a Bartholin cyst, small and asymptomatic, found at a routine visit. What is the best management?
options: Immediate excision of the gland
Marsupialization
Observation without treatment
Intravenous antibiotics
items.explanation: Small asymptomatic Bartholin duct cysts in a young woman need no treatment, since many resolve or remain stable, and intervention is reserved for painful, enlarging, or infected lesions. Excision and marsupialization carry bleeding, scarring, and dyspareunia risks that are unjustified. Antibiotics treat infection and do not shrink a sterile cyst. Women older than 40 with a new mass are biopsied for carcinoma.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman 12 days after laparoscopic hysterectomy has sudden vaginal pressure after lifting, with bowel visible at the introitus. What is the best initial step?
options: Push the bowel back in and discharge on pelvic rest
Place a vaginal pessary to support the cuff
Observe with serial examinations for 24 hours
Moist saline gauze, then emergent repair
items.explanation: Vaginal cuff dehiscence with evisceration is a surgical emergency. The exposed bowel is protected with warm moist saline gauze, the patient is kept supine or in a head-down position, intravenous access and antibiotics are started, and she goes urgently to the operating room for repair and evaluation. Reduction and discharge risk strangulation and peritonitis. A pessary and observation both delay needed repair.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman is having a vaginal hysterectomy for prolapse. The surgeon clamps the uterine vessels close to the cervix. Which structure lies closest, passing beneath the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix?
options: Round ligament
Pudendal nerve
Ureter
Obturator artery
items.explanation: The ureter passes under the uterine artery roughly 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix, which is why it is vulnerable to clamping and ligation at this point. Keeping clamps close to the cervix and applying downward traction reduces risk. The round ligament runs anteriorly to the inguinal canal. The pudendal nerve is in the pudendal canal, and the obturator artery runs along the pelvic sidewall.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman is scheduled for major abdominal surgery lasting more than three hours for ovarian cancer. She has no bleeding risk and normal renal function. Which VTE prophylaxis is most appropriate?
options: Early ambulation alone without drug or mechanical measures
Compression devices plus anticoagulation for weeks
Graduated compression stockings alone until discharge
Low-dose aspirin for one week after the operation
items.explanation: Major cancer surgery in a woman over 40 places her in the highest risk category, so both mechanical compression and pharmacologic prophylaxis are recommended, with extended treatment up to four weeks after surgery for cancer. Ambulation alone suits low-risk cases. Stockings alone are insufficient at high risk. Aspirin is not an accepted stand-alone strategy for this risk level.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman is undergoing hysteroscopy with a bipolar resectoscope and normal saline as distending medium. The fluid deficit reaches 2.5 L, and she becomes hypertensive with dyspnea and crackles. What is the best explanation?
options: Fluid overload from absorbed isotonic medium
Dilutional hyponatremia from glycine
Hyperammonemia
Gas embolism from carbon dioxide
items.explanation: Absorbed isotonic saline expands intravascular volume and causes pulmonary edema, and a deficit above about 2.5 L in a healthy patient should stop the case, with loop diuretic and respiratory support. Sodium stays near normal because the fluid is isotonic. Hyponatremia and hyperammonemia belong to glycine. Gas embolism produces sudden hypotension and a drop in end-tidal carbon dioxide, not crackles.

items.stem: During an abdominal hysterectomy a 2 cm laceration of the bladder dome is recognized. The trigone and ureteral orifices are uninvolved. What is the best management?
options: Observation without repair
One-layer nonabsorbable closure without a catheter
Two-layer absorbable closure with catheter drainage for about 7 days
Bilateral ureteral stent placement as the only measure
items.explanation: A recognized dome cystotomy away from the trigone is repaired in two layers with absorbable suture, then drained with a urethral catheter for about seven days to allow healing. Leaving it alone invites urinoma and peritonitis. Nonabsorbable suture in the bladder promotes stones, and omitting a catheter risks leakage. Stents protect the ureters but do not close a bladder defect.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G1P0 woman at 17 weeks has painless cervical dilation to 3 cm with bulging membranes and no contractions, bleeding, or fever. What is the best treatment?
options: Expectant management with bed rest alone
Physical examination indicated cerclage
Immediate induction of labor
Progesterone supplementation alone
items.explanation: Painless dilation in the second trimester without infection or labor is the setting for rescue cerclage placed on examination findings, after excluding intraamniotic infection. Bed rest alone does not support a dilated cervix. Induction abandons a potentially salvageable pregnancy. Progesterone alone has not been shown to reverse existing dilation, so it is not enough as sole therapy at this stage.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman on postoperative day 2 after a colpopexy has abdominal distention, nausea, and no flatus. Bowel sounds are diminished, tenderness is mild and diffuse, and she has passed no stool. Radiographs show diffuse gas in small bowel and colon. Which management is best?
options: Immediate exploratory laparotomy
Oral laxatives with a regular diet
Intravenous antibiotics for presumed peritonitis
Bowel rest, electrolyte correction, and minimizing opioids
items.explanation: Diffuse gas throughout both small and large bowel after surgery indicates ileus, which is managed conservatively with limited oral intake, replacement of potassium and magnesium, early ambulation, and opioid reduction. Laparotomy is for obstruction that fails conservative care or for peritonitis. Laxatives and a regular diet worsen distention. Antibiotics do not treat a physiologic motility problem without signs of infection.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman recovering from an abdominal hysterectomy has a surgical drain removed and, on postoperative day 5, passes clear fluid continuously from the vagina. A tampon test after instilling dye into the bladder stains the tampon blue. What is the diagnosis?
options: Vesicovaginal fistula
Ureterovaginal fistula
Stress urinary incontinence
Vaginal cuff cellulitis
items.explanation: Continuous leakage after hysterectomy with dye instilled into the bladder appearing on a vaginal tampon indicates a communication between bladder and vagina. A ureterovaginal fistula would leave the tampon unstained by retrograde bladder dye, since urine enters the vagina from above, and would require an oral or intravenous dye to show. Stress incontinence causes leakage with effort only, and cellulitis gives pain, fever, and discharge.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at laparoscopy for an ovarian cyst has bleeding from a lateral port site, with blood dripping along the cannula. What is the best initial step to control it?
options: Remove the cannula and observe the site
Increase insufflation pressure to compress it
Balloon catheter tamponade through the port
Apply a pressure bandage over the skin site
items.explanation: Bleeding from the lateral port site suggests injury to the inferior epigastric vessel, and tamponade with a Foley balloon inflated and pulled against the abdominal wall controls it until a suture ligature is placed. Removing the cannula without tamponade can allow hematoma formation. Raising intraabdominal pressure does not compress the deep vessel. Skin dressings cannot stop bleeding from beneath the muscle.

items.stem: During operative hysteroscopy for a type 1 myoma with glycine distention, the fluid deficit reaches 2.4 L. The patient becomes confused and the serum sodium returns at 118 mEq/L. What is the best next step?
options: Continue and finish the resection quickly to limit operative time
Stop, check electrolytes, and give furosemide with slow sodium correction
Infuse hypotonic fluid to dilute the glycine load
Give rapid hypertonic saline to correct sodium to 140 mEq/L within an hour
items.explanation: Absorption of electrolyte-free glycine has produced symptomatic hyponatremia with a large deficit, so the procedure is halted at once, labs are repeated, and a loop diuretic is given while sodium is corrected slowly. Finishing the case worsens absorption. Hypotonic fluid deepens the dilution. Overly rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination, so the rise is limited to a modest rate per day.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has abnormal uterine bleeding for 8 months and an endometrial thickness of 14 mm. She has no hormonal use and is not pregnant. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Office endometrial biopsy
Reassurance and repeat ultrasonography in one year
Immediate hysterectomy without tissue diagnosis
Cervical cytology alone
items.explanation: Women aged 45 or older with abnormal uterine bleeding need endometrial sampling to exclude hyperplasia or carcinoma, and a thickened lining adds to the concern. Office biopsy is quick and has high detection for diffuse disease. Waiting a year delays a possible cancer diagnosis. Removing the uterus before tissue diagnosis can lead to incorrect surgery. Cervical cytology screens the cervix and does not evaluate the endometrium.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman with menorrhagia has a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL and an MCV of 72 fL. Hysterectomy is planned in three weeks. What is the best preoperative step?
options: Transfuse two units of red cells the week before surgery
Start erythropoietin without further evaluation
Cancel the operation until hemoglobin reaches 13 g/dL
Check ferritin and begin iron replacement
items.explanation: Microcytic anemia from chronic blood loss is most often iron deficiency, so confirming with ferritin and replacing iron (oral or intravenous) for the available weeks improves hemoglobin and lowers transfusion risk. Elective transfusion exposes her to avoidable risk. Erythropoietin is ineffective when iron is lacking. Postponing indefinitely is unnecessary, because surgery may proceed once treatment is under way and the response is documented.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman undergoing laparoscopic hysterectomy develops a full-thickness skin burn beneath the dispersive electrode pad on her thigh. What is the most likely cause?
options: Excessive bipolar current delivered at the pedicle
Poor pad contact concentrating the return current
Reflection of laser energy from a surgical instrument
Stray ultrasonic vibration from the shears
items.explanation: In monopolar surgery the current must return through the dispersive pad, and a pad that is folded, wrinkled, partly lifted, or placed over scar or hair concentrates current and burns skin. Bipolar current passes between the jaws and does not involve a return pad. Laser reflection injures eyes and tissue near the beam, and ultrasonic shears act by vibration without a return pathway.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a hemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL after a postoperative hemorrhage and refuses blood transfusion on religious grounds. She is hemodynamically stable. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Transfuse because the hemoglobin is below 8 g/dL now
Transfuse under the emergency exception to consent
Respect her refusal and conserve blood
Seek a court order to authorize the transfusion
items.explanation: A competent adult may refuse transfusion, and the physician must respect that choice while maximizing alternatives such as intravenous iron, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, minimizing phlebotomy, and cell salvage when she accepts it. Giving blood against her wishes is battery. Sedating her to override consent is unethical. Court orders are for minors or incapacitated patients, not competent adults.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman had an incomplete abortion treated with suction curettage 6 months ago and now has amenorrhea with cyclic pelvic pain and a normal pregnancy test. Hysterosalpingography shows a filling defect pattern consistent with synechiae. What is the best treatment?
options: Repeat blind curettage of the cavity
Long-term oral contraceptives alone for months
Hysterectomy for definitive treatment
Operative hysteroscopic lysis of adhesions
items.explanation: Intrauterine adhesions after curettage cause amenorrhea or hypomenorrhea and pain, and the best treatment is direct visualization with hysteroscopic division of adhesions followed by measures to prevent recurrence. Blind curettage can worsen scarring. Hormones alone cannot divide fibrous bands. Hysterectomy is excessive in a young woman who may desire fertility. It would also remove any possibility of pregnancy.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has dilation and curettage under hysteroscopic guidance. The surgeon notices a smooth lateral defect while advancing a blunt dilator and no energy device was activated. She is stable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop, observe, and perform serial examinations
Immediate laparotomy with hysterectomy
Continue curettage to complete the sampling
Perform laparoscopy only if the pulse exceeds 120
items.explanation: A fundal or lateral perforation made with a blunt instrument in a stable patient usually heals and can be observed with vital signs and abdominal examinations, after stopping the procedure. Hysterectomy is excessive for a small uncomplicated defect. Continuing instrumentation risks widening the injury and injuring adjacent viscera. Laparoscopic inspection is reserved for unstable patients or perforation with a suction or energy instrument.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a laser used for vulvar condyloma ablation. Which measure is part of standard laser safety?
options: Dry drapes only near the beam
High oxygen concentrations at the field
Eye protection for all in the room
Turning off the smoke evacuator to cut noise
items.explanation: Laser safety includes wavelength-appropriate eye protection for everyone in the room, wet drapes or towels around the field, a smoke evacuator to remove infectious plume, and signage on the door. Dry drapes ignite readily. High oxygen concentrations increase fire risk. Removing the evacuator exposes the team to plume that can carry viral particles and irritants.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman is scheduled for abdominal hysterectomy. She weighs 130 kg. Which cefazolin dose is appropriate for surgical prophylaxis?
options: 1 g intravenously within 60 minutes before incision
3 g intravenously within 60 minutes before incision
2 g intravenously within 60 minutes before incision
2 g orally the night before surgery
items.explanation: Cefazolin prophylaxis is weight adjusted, at 2 g for most patients and 3 g for those weighing 120 kg or more, given within 60 minutes before incision so tissue levels are adequate. A 1 g dose is subtherapeutic. Two grams is correct for patients under 120 kg. Oral dosing the night before does not achieve tissue concentrations at incision.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman reports 10 days after loop electrosurgical excision for CIN 3 heavy vaginal bleeding soaking a pad each hour. She is stable. What is the best first step?
options: Exam with topical hemostatic agent or suture
Repeat excision of the entire transformation zone
Immediate hysterectomy for uncontrolled bleeding
Reassure and have her return in a week
items.explanation: Delayed hemorrhage 7 to 14 days after loop excision results from sloughing of the eschar, and it is usually controlled by examination with direct pressure, a topical agent such as ferric subsulfate paste, silver nitrate, or sutures. Repeating the excision causes more bleeding. Hysterectomy is excessive. Heavy bleeding that soaks a pad hourly is not safe to observe without intervention.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has an endometrial biopsy with a Pipelle device for abnormal bleeding while on a combined contraceptive. Which statement about the procedure is correct?
options: It is the most accurate way to diagnose fibroids
It requires general anesthesia
It always removes focal polyps completely
A positive pregnancy test must be excluded first
items.explanation: Pregnancy must be ruled out before sampling the endometrium because the device can disturb a gestation. Biopsy diagnoses hyperplasia and cancer with good accuracy when disease is diffuse, but it is not the best test for fibroids and can miss focal lesions such as polyps. It is performed in the office with little or no anesthesia.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman is scheduled for a 90-minute laparoscopic procedure and has an elevated Caprini score from age, obesity, and prolonged surgery. She also has a history of provoked deep venous thrombosis. Which prophylaxis is best?
options: Compression plus anticoagulation
Early ambulation with no other measures
Graduated compression stockings alone
No prophylaxis given short operative time
items.explanation: A prior venous thrombosis combined with other risk factors places her at higher risk, so mechanical and pharmacologic methods are combined, with attention to bleeding risk. Ambulation or stockings alone suit low-risk patients. Operative duration is only one component of the score, and a short case does not erase a history of thrombosis. Prophylaxis continues until she walks freely.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has sharp burning pain and numbness along the lower lateral edge of a Pfannenstiel incision, worse with standing, 3 weeks after cesarean delivery. Pain resolves briefly after local anesthetic infiltration at the pain point. What is the diagnosis?
options: Rectus sheath hematoma
Ilioinguinal nerve entrapment
Femoral neuropathy from retractor pressure
Incisional hernia with nerve irritation
items.explanation: Entrapment of the ilioinguinal or iliohypogastric nerve in a fascial suture or scar causes localized neuropathic pain near the lateral incision, with relief after infiltration with local anesthetic confirming the diagnosis. A rectus sheath hematoma gives a tender mass and a falling hemoglobin early. Femoral neuropathy weakens the quadriceps. Incisional hernia produces a bulge that enlarges with straining and not isolated burning pain.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with menorrhagia and a normal endometrial biopsy and uterine cavity wants a minimally invasive treatment and has completed childbearing. Which condition is a contraindication to endometrial ablation?
options: Regular heavy cycles
Prior vaginal deliveries
Normal cavity on sonohysterography
Desire for future pregnancy
items.explanation: Endometrial ablation is meant for women who have completed childbearing, because pregnancy after ablation is dangerous with high rates of loss, preterm birth, and abnormal placentation. Heavy regular bleeding is the main indication. Prior deliveries do not matter. A normal cavity is a requirement for most devices, along with a normal biopsy, so none of these precludes the procedure.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a total fluid deficit of 1.2 L during resectoscopic myomectomy with a nonelectrolyte medium. She is awake under spinal anesthesia and develops nausea and headache. Which solution is the correct medium for a monopolar resectoscope?
options: Normal saline solution
Lactated Ringer solution, warmed
Sorbitol or glycine solution
Any isotonic electrolyte solution
items.explanation: Monopolar current is conducted through the tissue and would disperse in a saline medium, so monopolar resectoscopes require electrolyte-free fluids such as glycine, sorbitol, or mannitol. These are hypotonic and risk hyponatremia, which is why careful deficit tracking matters. Saline and lactated Ringer solution conduct current and are used with bipolar instruments, where overload causes volume problems rather than hyponatremia.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a temperature of 38.5 C on postoperative day 4 after abdominal hysterectomy with new calf pain and swelling, and the wound and urine are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Compression duplex ultrasonography of the leg
Chest radiography as the only test
Observation until the fever resolves on its own
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging urgently
items.explanation: Fever with unilateral calf pain and swelling days after pelvic surgery suggests deep venous thrombosis, which is confirmed by compression duplex ultrasonography before anticoagulation. Chest films alone would miss the leg source. Waiting risks pulmonary embolism. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging looks for abscess and does not explain calf findings. Treatment starts promptly once thrombosis is confirmed.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman requires cesarean hysterectomy for placenta accreta spectrum with massive hemorrhage. Which step best reduces ureteral injury?
options: Clamp en masse across the broad ligament quickly
Ligate the uterine arteries far lateral to the cervix
Perform hysterectomy through a vertical vaginal incision
Identify the ureters and free the bladder first
items.explanation: Distorted anatomy and engorged vessels in placenta accreta increase ureteral injury, so the surgeon identifies the ureter, develops the bladder plane away from the lower segment, and places clamps close to the uterus. Blind clamping is hazardous. Placing ties lateral to the cervix is where the ureter runs beneath the artery. A vaginal incision does not apply to cesarean hysterectomy.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman wants sterilization and asks about failure rates and the types of pregnancy that could result. Which counseling statement is correct?
options: Failure is impossible once occlusion is complete
Ectopic is a large share of failures
Failure risk is highest among the oldest women
Failures never occur after a decade
items.explanation: No method is perfect, with a ten-year cumulative failure risk of nearly two percent after tubal sterilization, higher in younger women, and when pregnancy occurs a substantial share is ectopic, so early evaluation is advised. Failure is possible years later because tubes may recanalize or fistulize. The risk is highest in the youngest women, not older ones, and it persists over time.

items.stem: A surgeon is placing an accessory trocar during laparoscopy and wants to avoid the inferior epigastric vessels. Which site is safest?
options: Medial to the rectus lateral border at the midclavicular line
Directly in the midline below the umbilicus
Lateral to the lateral border of the rectus muscle
Immediately beneath the rectus muscle belly
items.explanation: The inferior epigastric vessels run along the deep surface of the rectus, medial to the lateral rectus edge, so ports placed lateral to that edge, under direct vision and with transillumination, avoid them. Placement medial to the lateral border risks injury. The midline below the umbilicus avoids them but is a different landmark. Penetrating beneath the rectus belly crosses the vessels.

items.stem: A 34-year-old nonpregnant woman has biopsy-confirmed CIN 2 after high-grade cytology and a satisfactory colposcopy. What is the recommended management?
options: Treatment with either excision or ablation
Repeat cytology and human papillomavirus testing in 12 months
Hysterectomy as the standard treatment
Observation only, because CIN 2 regresses in all adults
items.explanation: In a nonpregnant woman aged 25 or older, CIN 2 or 3 with a satisfactory colposcopy is treated, either by excision such as loop excision or by ablation, because progression risk justifies intervention. Repeat testing alone is surveillance suited to lower-grade disease. Hysterectomy is excessive for this diagnosis. Observation is reserved for selected young women or pregnancy, and it is not offered to every adult.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has weak knee extension and difficulty climbing stairs after an abdominal hysterectomy performed with a self-retaining retractor that had deep side blades. Which nerve was most likely injured?
options: Common peroneal nerve
Femoral nerve
Obturator nerve
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
items.explanation: A deep side blade of a self-retaining retractor can compress the femoral nerve against the psoas muscle, and extreme hip flexion can stretch it, so the quadriceps fails and the knee cannot extend. The common peroneal nerve produces foot drop after compression at the fibular head. The obturator nerve is injured in lymph node dissection or by extreme flexion with abduction. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve causes numbness without weakness.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman receives lidocaine 1% for a paracervical block before dilation and evacuation. She develops perioral numbness, tinnitus, and then a seizure. What is the best treatment after airway support?
options: Intravenous calcium gluconate
Intravenous naloxone
Intravenous flumazenil
Intravenous lipid emulsion
items.explanation: Perioral numbness, tinnitus, and seizure after local anesthetic infiltration indicate systemic toxicity, which is treated with airway and seizure control and an intravenous lipid emulsion that sequesters the drug. Calcium gluconate is used for magnesium toxicity. Naloxone reverses opioids, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, neither of which is the cause here. Lipid therapy is given alongside airway and seizure control.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman with a body mass index of 31 is having surgery under enhanced recovery principles. Which element is part of such a pathway?
options: Prolonged fasting from midnight
Routine mechanical bowel preparation
Carbohydrate drink until two hours before anesthesia
Routine nasogastric tube after surgery
items.explanation: Enhanced recovery pathways avoid long fasting by allowing clear carbohydrate fluids until two hours before anesthesia, and add multimodal analgesia, early feeding, early mobilization, and prompt catheter removal. Fasting from midnight and routine bowel preparation worsen dehydration without lowering infection in most gynecologic cases. Nasogastric tubes are used selectively and are not routine in modern recovery protocols.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has a spinal anesthetic for cesarean and develops a positional headache on day 2 that improves lying flat. Conservative care fails after 48 hours. Which treatment is most effective?
options: Lumbar puncture to measure pressure
Intravenous antibiotics
Repeat spinal injection
Epidural blood patch
items.explanation: A headache worse upright and relieved supine after dural puncture indicates cerebrospinal fluid leak. When fluids, caffeine, and analgesics fail, an epidural blood patch seals the defect with high success. A diagnostic lumbar puncture would add another dural hole. Antibiotics treat meningitis, which presents with fever and neck stiffness. A repeat spinal injection would worsen the leak.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has symptomatic fibroids and is scheduled for laparoscopic myomectomy. She takes warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve. Which perioperative approach is most appropriate?
options: Continue warfarin at the usual dose through surgery
Stop warfarin and bridge with parenteral therapy
Stop warfarin with no bridging anticoagulation
Replace warfarin with low-dose aspirin alone
items.explanation: A mechanical mitral valve carries a high thromboembolic risk, so warfarin is stopped about five days before surgery and a short-acting parenteral anticoagulant is used until shortly before and soon after the operation. Continuing the drug at full effect risks major surgical bleeding. Interrupting it without cover exposes the valve to thrombosis. Aspirin does not provide adequate protection for a mechanical valve.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman has a 35 pack-year smoking history, scheduled elective hysterectomy in 6 weeks. Which counseling about tobacco is most appropriate?
options: Quitting 4 weeks beforehand lowers complications
Stopping now increases surgical risk and should be delayed
Smoking has no meaningful effect on wound healing
Cessation matters only for patients over 65 years
items.explanation: Smoking impairs oxygen delivery and collagen formation, raising infection, dehiscence, and pulmonary complications, and cessation for at least four weeks before surgery measurably lowers these risks. The notion that quitting suddenly harms surgical outcome is a myth. Healing effects occur at any age. Cessation support with counseling and pharmacotherapy should begin at once. Surgery need not be postponed to allow it.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has a Bartholin gland abscess, 4 cm and fluctuant, drained for the first time. Which treatment best lowers the chance of recurrence?
options: Simple incision without any packing
Immediate excision of the gland
Placement of a Word catheter for several weeks
Oral antibiotics alone
items.explanation: After incision, a Word balloon catheter left in for about four weeks allows an epithelialized tract to form and reduces recurrence. Simple incision and drainage alone often closes and reaccumulates. Excision is reserved for recurrent or persistent cases because of bleeding and scarring. Antibiotics alone cannot empty a loculated collection, and they are mainly useful with cellulitis or specific infection.

items.stem: During a cesarean delivery, the bladder flap is being developed. Dissection in which plane best avoids bladder injury?
options: Loose plane beneath the vesicouterine fold
Deep within the myometrium behind the bladder wall
Through the anterior vaginal wall at the cervix level
Within the bladder wall muscle
items.explanation: The bladder is separated from the lower uterine segment by developing the loose areolar plane beneath the vesicouterine peritoneal fold, using sharp and blunt dissection, and the fold is lifted to stay clear of the bladder. Dissecting inside the myometrium risks uterine laceration. A vaginal approach is not part of cesarean technique. Cutting into bladder muscle is the injury being avoided.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has postmenopausal bleeding and a transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 3 mm. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Immediate hysterectomy
Dilation and curettage under anesthesia
Endometrial ablation
Reassurance with follow-up if bleeding persists
items.explanation: A thickness of 4 mm or less with a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding carries a very low risk of cancer, so observation is acceptable, with biopsy if bleeding recurs or persists. Hysterectomy and curettage are unnecessary invasive steps. Ablation is not a treatment for postmenopausal bleeding and may conceal later disease. She should be told to return if any further bleeding occurs.

items.stem: A 51-year-old woman with a history of coronary stent placement 18 months ago on aspirin alone needs hysterectomy for fibroids. How should aspirin be managed perioperatively?
options: Stop aspirin for 10 days before surgery
Continue aspirin through the perioperative period
Stop aspirin and start warfarin
Replace aspirin with a nonsteroidal drug
items.explanation: Patients with coronary stents are at risk of stent thrombosis when antiplatelet therapy is stopped, and low-dose aspirin is generally continued because surgical bleeding is manageable. Stopping it for 10 days is the choice used when the indication is only primary prevention. Switching to warfarin does not protect a stent. A nonsteroidal drug lacks the same platelet effect and adds bleeding and renal risks.

items.stem: A patient undergoing hysteroscopy has an electrosurgical loop that is activated while she is in contact with the metal stirrup, resulting in a burn. Which principle of electrosurgical safety was violated?
options: Using the lowest setting on bipolar forceps
Ensuring isotonic distending medium
Avoiding alternate return pathways for monopolar current
Limiting activation time near the ureter
items.explanation: Monopolar current seeks any path back to the generator, and contact with grounded metal can concentrate it and burn skin, so patients are insulated from metal and a properly applied return electrode is used. Bipolar settings and activation limits are separate safety measures. Isotonic medium is wrong for monopolar devices, which require electrolyte-free fluid, but it does not explain a contact burn at the stirrup.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman has chronic pelvic pain and undergoes laparoscopy. Entry at the umbilicus is complicated by dense periumbilical adhesions from prior laparotomies. Which alternative entry site is recommended?
options: Palmer point in the left upper quadrant
Suprapubic midline just above the symphysis
Lateral flank near the iliac crest
Posterior cul-de-sac by colpotomy
items.explanation: When prior midline surgery makes umbilical entry hazardous, Palmer point, about 3 cm below the left costal margin in the midclavicular line, is a standard alternative because adhesions are uncommon there, provided the stomach is decompressed. A suprapubic entry places the bladder and pelvic structures at risk. A flank entry has no benefit. The posterior cul-de-sac is a vaginal approach and not a laparoscopic port site.

items.stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 woman at 14 weeks has a history of one painless second-trimester loss at 19 weeks without other cause. A transvaginal ultrasound shows a closed cervix measuring 31 mm. Which management is appropriate?
options: Immediate emergency cerclage
Pessary placement in all cases
History-indicated cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks
Termination of the pregnancy
items.explanation: A history of one or more second-trimester losses with painless dilation and no other cause supports history-indicated cerclage, placed electively at the end of the first trimester or early second. Emergency placement is for found dilation. Pessaries are not first-line for this indication. Termination is not warranted because the current cervix is closed and the pregnancy is healthy, with a good outcome likely after support.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman takes lisinopril and metformin for hypertension and diabetes and is scheduled for hysterectomy the next morning. Which instruction is most appropriate?
options: Take both drugs as usual and eat breakfast
Hold metformin, and consider holding lisinopril
Stop all of her medications for one week before
Double the metformin dose on the day before surgery
items.explanation: Metformin is held the day of surgery because of lactic acidosis risk if kidney perfusion falls and she will be fasting, while an ACE inhibitor is often held about 24 hours earlier to limit intraoperative hypotension. Taking both without thought risks these problems. Stopping every medication for a week is unnecessary and removes blood pressure control. Doubling metformin is hazardous.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman on postoperative day 7 after an abdominal hysterectomy has a 38.2 C fever and a swollen, red, tender incision with purulent drainage. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the best management?
options: Close the wound tightly and give oral antibiotics only
Begin therapeutic anticoagulation for presumed pelvic thrombosis
Order immediate exploratory laparotomy for deep infection
Open and drain the wound; add antibiotics if cellulitis spreads
items.explanation: A superficial surgical site infection with purulent drainage is treated by opening the incision, evacuating pus, and local wound care, with antibiotics added when erythema extends beyond the margins or systemic signs are present. Tight closure traps infection. Anticoagulation addresses thrombosis, not an infected wound. Laparotomy is warranted for deep infection, fascial separation, or necrotizing disease, none of which is described.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman 10 days after total laparoscopic hysterectomy has flank pain, fever, and rising creatinine. Computed tomography with delayed contrast images shows hydronephrosis and extravasation near the pelvic sidewall. What is the best next step?
options: Stent or nephrostomy with urology consultation
Observation with oral antibiotics and repeat labs
Immediate repeat laparotomy without any drainage
Start loop diuretics with fluid restriction
items.explanation: Delayed ureteral injury with hydronephrosis and leak is managed first by decompression, either retrograde stenting or nephrostomy, with definitive repair planned by urology if the stent cannot be passed. Antibiotics alone leave an obstructed, leaking system. Immediate open surgery in an infected field is deferred. Diuretics and restriction do not address a mechanical injury and may worsen renal function.

items.stem: A patient is undergoing a pelvic procedure under general anesthesia. Fire erupts on the drapes near the surgical field. After stopping gas flow and removing burning material, what is the immediate priority?
options: Continue the operation while extinguishing the drapes
Remove the tube and circuit if airway involved
Increase oxygen flow to the surgical field
Apply more flammable prep solution to the field
items.explanation: In an airway fire the team stops gas flow, removes the tube and any burning material, and extinguishes the fire, then ventilates and examines the airway. Continuing the case endangers the patient. Higher oxygen feeds the flames, and flammable skin preparation is a classic ignition source and fuel. Risk is reduced by letting prep solutions dry fully and keeping the oxygen fraction low near electrosurgery.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman who underwent cesarean delivery for labor arrest at 4 cm after rupture of membranes for 20 hours asks about infection prevention. Which prophylaxis is best?
options: Cefazolin alone after cord clamping
Ceftriaxone for three days after delivery
Cefazolin plus azithromycin before skin incision
No antibiotics unless fever develops
items.explanation: For cesarean delivery in labor or with ruptured membranes, adding azithromycin to cefazolin before the skin incision lowers endometritis and wound infection, and a weight of 120 kg or more calls for a 3 g cefazolin dose. Giving cefazolin alone after cord clamping is outdated and less effective. Prolonged postoperative antibiotics add no benefit. Waiting for fever delays treatment of an avoidable infection.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman has a multimodal pain plan after abdominal hysterectomy. Which approach best reflects opioid stewardship at discharge?
options: A 30-day opioid supply for breakthrough pain
Opioids alone, with no other analgesics given
No analgesic at discharge
Nonopioids plus a short opioid course
items.explanation: Opioid stewardship pairs scheduled nonopioid agents such as acetaminophen and nonsteroidal drugs with a limited opioid supply, often a few days, for breakthrough pain, with disposal counseling. A month of opioids increases dependence and diversion. Opioids alone leave pain undertreated and dose heavy. Sending a patient home without analgesia ignores expected postoperative pain. Instructions on safe storage and disposal complete the plan.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman is receiving a preoperative cardiac assessment before hysterectomy for endometrial cancer. She can climb two flights of stairs without symptoms. How should her functional capacity be classified?
options: Poor, at fewer than four metabolic equivalents
Unknown, requiring a stress test first
Adequate, at four metabolic equivalents or more
Absolute contraindication to surgery
items.explanation: The ability to climb two flights of stairs corresponds to at least four metabolic equivalents, an adequate functional capacity that allows most patients with no active cardiac condition to proceed without further testing. Poor capacity is under four, such as being unable to climb a flight. Stress testing is not required when capacity is adequate and no active condition exists. Nothing in the history suggests a contraindication.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a 4 cm Bartholin abscess that recurs after catheter placement twice asks about definitive management. What is the best option?
options: Repeat needle aspiration every week
Long-term suppressive oral antibiotics
Silver nitrate cautery of the gland duct
Marsupialization or gland excision
items.explanation: Recurrent abscess after drainage and catheter treatment is managed with marsupialization, which creates a permanent drainage opening, or with excision of the gland in selected cases. A biopsy is also considered at her age to exclude carcinoma. Repeated aspiration and suppressive antibiotics do not create a lasting tract. Silver nitrate has no role in treating a deep gland collection.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has a suction dilation and curettage for a missed abortion and the aspirator passes unusually deeply, with omentum visible in the aspirate. She is stable. What is the best next step?
options: Continue the procedure and discharge
Laparoscopy to inspect for bowel injury
Observe overnight with no further evaluation
Give misoprostol to complete the evacuation
items.explanation: Visible bowel or omentum in the suction aspirate means the uterus has been perforated with an active instrument and viscera may be injured, so laparoscopy or laparotomy is needed to inspect and repair any damage. Continuing instrumentation increases harm. Observation alone can miss mesenteric bleeding or bowel injury. Misoprostol does not address perforation. Delay allows peritonitis to develop.

items.stem: In a patient receiving general anesthesia, an unexpected sudden fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide and hypotension occur during hysteroscopy distended with carbon dioxide gas. What is the most likely cause?
options: Gas embolism
Hyponatremia from absorbed distending fluid
Malignant hyperthermia
Anaphylaxis to latex
items.explanation: A sudden drop in end-tidal carbon dioxide with hypotension during gas insufflation suggests venous gas embolism, which obstructs pulmonary flow. Management is to stop insufflation, flood the field, place the patient left side down and head down, and give oxygen. Hyponatremia occurs with hypotonic liquid media and develops over a longer course. Malignant hyperthermia raises carbon dioxide, and anaphylaxis causes bronchospasm and rash.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a positive endocervical curettage and an unsatisfactory colposcopy after high-grade cytology needs further evaluation. Which procedure is most appropriate?
options: Repeat colposcopy and cytology in six months
Diagnostic cold knife conization
Cryotherapy of the entire ectocervix today
Endometrial biopsy with sampling of the lining
items.explanation: An unsatisfactory colposcopy cannot exclude disease hidden in the canal, and a positive endocervical sample adds to the concern, so a diagnostic excision provides tissue for pathology. Repeating colposcopy leaves the lesion unassessed. Cryotherapy destroys tissue without a specimen and is inappropriate before a diagnosis. Endometrial biopsy samples the uterine lining, which is unrelated to cervical disease.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with a body mass index of 41 and prior midline laparotomies needs a pelvic mass resection. Which feature favors a vertical midline incision over a Pfannenstiel incision?
options: Lower rates of incisional hernia and wound dehiscence
Less postoperative incisional pain and faster recovery
A scar hidden below the bikini line for cosmesis
Quick entry with wide upper abdominal exposure
items.explanation: A vertical midline incision through the linea alba is quick, relatively bloodless, and extends upward for staging or unexpected findings, which suits a pelvic mass of uncertain nature. Its drawbacks are higher hernia and dehiscence rates, more pain, and a visible scar. Pfannenstiel incisions are better for cosmesis and hernia prevention but limit upper abdominal exposure and are hard to extend in obesity.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman is receiving an oral anticoagulant that is a direct factor Xa inhibitor and needs elective surgery with a high bleeding risk, with normal renal function. When should the drug be stopped?
options: On the morning of the operation
Two full weeks before the operation
About two days before surgery
It should not be stopped at all
items.explanation: Direct oral anticoagulants have short half-lives, so for a high bleeding risk procedure and normal renal function they are held about two days beforehand, without bridging. Stopping the same morning leaves a full anticoagulant effect. Two weeks is unnecessarily long and raises thrombotic risk. Continuing the drug invites major surgical bleeding. This timing applies with normal kidney function.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman is on a chronic prednisone dose of 15 mg daily for polymyalgia and needs major gynecologic surgery. What perioperative steroid approach is appropriate?
options: Give stress-dose glucocorticoids around the time of surgery
Stop prednisone the week before
Give no steroid on the day of surgery
Start dexamethasone only if she becomes hypotensive
items.explanation: Long-term prednisone suppresses the adrenal axis, so patients receive perioperative supplementation, often with hydrocortisone, to prevent adrenal crisis during surgical stress. Stopping the drug invites crisis and disease flare. Omitting a dose on the day of surgery does the same. Waiting for hypotension delays therapy that should be given prophylactically. The decision is made before incision, not during a crisis.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman needs hysterectomy for a 500 g fibroid uterus and a history of two cesarean deliveries. The surgeon discusses the risk of tissue morcellation. What is the main concern?
options: Higher rates of postoperative ileus
Increased risk of vault dehiscence
Reduced ovarian reserve
Dissemination of an unsuspected uterine sarcoma
items.explanation: Uncontained morcellation of a presumed fibroid can spread an occult leiomyosarcoma within the abdomen and worsen survival, which led to a regulatory warning. Contained bag morcellation, or avoiding morcellation when malignancy is suspected, is recommended. Ileus, cuff dehiscence, and ovarian reserve are unrelated to the morcellation concern, though each can matter in other aspects of hysterectomy.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has a transverse low uterine incision cesarean for breech presentation at 39 weeks with a body mass index of 44 and a subcutaneous layer of 4 cm. Which technique lowers wound complications?
options: Close the fat layer if 2 cm or thicker
Leave the subcutaneous space open to drain
Place a subcutaneous drain routinely
Use only skin staples without closing fat
items.explanation: Closure of the subcutaneous tissue when it measures 2 cm or more reduces seroma and disruption, and routine drains have not shown benefit. Leaving a deep space open invites fluid collection and infection. Staples alone ignore the dead space. Skin closure choice is separate, with either suture or staples acceptable, though staples are linked to somewhat more separation in obese women.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman had a total hysterectomy 2 days ago. She has had little urine output for 8 hours, with a heart rate of 118 beats per minute, a blood pressure of 88/52 mm Hg, and a falling hemoglobin from 11.2 to 7.9 g/dL. Pain is increasing and the abdomen is distended. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Postoperative ileus with distention
Intraabdominal hemorrhage
Urinary tract infection
Atelectasis
items.explanation: Hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria, a large drop in hemoglobin, and a distending abdomen indicate continued bleeding from a pedicle or vessel, which requires resuscitation and often return to the operating room. Ileus does not drop the hemoglobin or the pressure. A urinary infection does not cause shock. Atelectasis raises temperature and respiratory signs, without abdominal distention or anemia.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman requests hysterectomy for abnormal bleeding and a 12-week sized uterus. Which finding best supports choosing the vaginal route?
options: Suspected severe endometriosis with dense adhesions
Fixed uterus and narrow pubic arch
Mobile uterus with good vaginal access
Suspected ovarian cancer needing staging
items.explanation: Vaginal hysterectomy suits a mobile uterus with adequate vaginal capacity when the adnexa do not need extensive surgery. Severe endometriosis with adhesions, a fixed uterus, or a narrow pubic arch limits vaginal access and raises complication risk. Suspected ovarian cancer needs a laparotomy or laparoscopy for full staging, so the vaginal route would be inadequate.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman requests permanent contraception at the time of cesarean delivery. Which technique has the lowest risk of future ovarian cancer and ectopic pregnancy?
options: Bilateral salpingectomy
Bilateral tubal clips
Unipolar tubal coagulation
Hysteroscopic intratubal device
items.explanation: Removing both fallopian tubes eliminates ectopic pregnancy from the sterilized tubes and removes the site of origin for many high-grade serous cancers, so it is favored when feasible. Clips and coagulation leave tubal tissue and have a lifetime failure risk with a high share of ectopics. Hysteroscopic devices are not used at cesarean and have been withdrawn from the market in many places.

items.stem: During a difficult abdominal hysterectomy, bleeding arises from the presacral venous plexus while the surgeon mobilizes the rectosigmoid. Suction and pressure fail to control it. What is the best next step?
options: Ligate both internal iliac arteries immediately
Place sterile tacks into the sacrum over the veins
Pack the pelvis and close without further attempts
Apply bipolar cautery directly to the bleeding veins
items.explanation: Presacral veins retract into sacral bone foramina and bleed torrentially, so after pressure, the accepted rescue is to compress the bleeding point with sterile titanium tacks driven into the sacrum, or to use a muscle fragment. Internal iliac ligation does not stop this venous basivertebral bleeding. Packing alone may be a final measure but is not first. Cautery fails because veins sit in bone.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman has a temperature of 38.4 C on the first postoperative day after an abdominal hysterectomy. She is splinting, has diminished breath sounds at both bases, and her wound and urine are normal. What is the best next step?
options: Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Order computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
Incentive spirometry and early ambulation
Remove the urinary catheter and send blood cultures only
items.explanation: Fever in the first 48 hours is most often from atelectasis, particularly with shallow breathing from incisional pain. Deep breathing exercises, spirometry, adequate analgesia, and walking reopen alveoli and are first-line care. Antibiotics are not indicated without a source. Imaging is reserved for fever persisting beyond several days. Cultures and catheter removal address urinary causes, which appear later and are not suggested here.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman at laparoscopic hysterectomy is found to have a defect in the bladder dome after dissection. It is repaired in two layers. What is the appropriate postoperative management?
options: Remove the catheter right away
Discharge without a catheter after one night
Ureteral stenting as the only treatment
Catheter drainage for 7 to 14 days
items.explanation: A bladder dome injury recognized and repaired in two layers heals well with continuous catheter drainage for roughly one to two weeks, followed by a cystogram when leak is a concern. Removing the catheter immediately places tension on the fresh repair. Discharging without drainage risks leak and urinary ascites. Ureteral stents address ureteral injury, not a dome repair away from the trigone.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman undergoes laparoscopic hysterectomy and lysis of adhesions. On postoperative day 3 she has fever, tachycardia, worsening diffuse abdominal pain, and a rising white cell count. Which complication should be suspected?
options: Atelectasis
Unrecognized thermal bowel injury
Pelvic hematoma without infection
Urinary retention
items.explanation: Delayed fever, tachycardia, and escalating pain around days 2 to 5 after laparoscopy with adhesiolysis suggest an unrecognized bowel injury, often from thermal spread, which presents later than a sharp laceration. Evaluation with computed tomography and a low threshold for reexploration is indicated. Atelectasis peaks in the first 48 hours with pulmonary findings. Hematoma and retention do not cause progressive peritonitis.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with a body mass index of 38 and obstructive sleep apnea is scheduled for hysterectomy. Which perioperative strategy best lowers her pulmonary complication risk?
options: Continue CPAP, use regional blocks, and limit opioids
Cancel surgery until her body mass index is below 30
Use high-dose opioid infusions for postoperative comfort
Omit positive airway pressure to avoid aspiration
items.explanation: Obstructive sleep apnea raises the risk of postoperative hypoxia and respiratory depression, so she should bring and use her positive airway pressure device, receive opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, and be monitored with continuous oximetry. Delaying surgery for weight loss is unrealistic and unnecessary. Large opioid doses and omitting positive pressure each increase the likelihood of apnea and hypoxemia in the recovery period.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman underwent loop excision for CIN 2 and pathology reports CIN 2 at the endocervical margin. What is the recommended follow-up?
options: Return to routine screening in three years
Immediate hysterectomy for residual disease
No further follow-up because margins are irrelevant
Re-excision or six-month surveillance
items.explanation: A positive endocervical margin with CIN 2 or worse confers a higher residual risk, so either a repeat diagnostic excision or close surveillance with endocervical sampling and cotesting at about six months is recommended, depending on patient preference. Returning to routine screening ignores the residual risk. Hysterectomy is excessive for most patients. Stopping follow-up is unsafe.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman is on postoperative day 2 after a laparotomy for ovarian cancer. She has colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and high-pitched bowel sounds. Radiographs show dilated small bowel with air-fluid levels and no colonic gas. What is the best initial management?
options: Oral laxatives plus a prokinetic agent and regular diet
Immediate colonoscopy to decompress the bowel
Nasogastric suction, fluids, and monitoring
Resume a regular diet and discharge home today
items.explanation: A mechanical small bowel obstruction, most often from adhesions, is treated initially with nasogastric suction, fluid and electrolyte replacement, and monitoring for strangulation, with surgery for peritonitis, ischemia, or failure to resolve. Laxatives and a regular diet worsen vomiting and pressure. Colonoscopy is aimed at the colon, where gas is absent here, and carries perforation risk.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 16 weeks is being evaluated for cervical cerclage. Which finding is a contraindication to placement?
options: Prior cervical conization with a loop excision
Regular contractions with advanced dilation
A prior preterm birth at 28 weeks of gestation
Cervical length of 22 mm on a scan at 20 weeks
items.explanation: Active labor, vaginal bleeding, chorioamnionitis, and ruptured membranes are contraindications to cerclage because the stitch cannot stop labor and can worsen infection. Prior conization is a risk factor that may justify cerclage. A prior preterm birth below 34 weeks with a short cervix is an accepted indication. A length below 25 mm in such a patient supports placement.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman undergoing laparoscopic myomectomy is positioned in steep Trendelenburg with shoulder braces. After 4 hours she has weakness of shoulder abduction and numbness over the lateral arm. What is the most likely injury?
options: Common peroneal compression
Femoral nerve compression
Pudendal neuropathy
Brachial plexus stretch
items.explanation: Steep head-down tilt with shoulder braces placed against the neck and acromion stretches or compresses the brachial plexus and causes arm weakness and numbness. Padding and positioning the braces over the acromioclavicular joint prevent it. Peroneal and femoral injuries affect the leg. Pudendal neuropathy causes perineal numbness and is associated with traction during vaginal procedures.

items.stem: A 48-year-old G3P3 woman with symptomatic fibroids has a mobile uterus of about 150 g, no prior abdominal surgery, and good vaginal descent. She asks which hysterectomy route is generally preferred for her. What is the best answer?
options: Total abdominal hysterectomy through a low transverse incision
Robotic-assisted hysterectomy as the first-line route
Vaginal hysterectomy
Supracervical hysterectomy by laparotomy
items.explanation: When feasible, vaginal hysterectomy is the preferred route because it has the lowest morbidity and cost, with laparoscopic next and abdominal reserved for cases that cannot be done by a minimally invasive route. A mobile, modest-sized uterus with descent favors the vaginal route. Robotic surgery adds cost without benefit here. Laparotomy carries more pain and longer recovery, and supracervical removal is not chosen for route reasons.

items.stem: During a Pfannenstiel cesarean delivery closure, a surgeon wants to avoid the vessels that lie deep to the rectus muscle in the lateral part of the incision. Which vessels are these?
options: Inferior epigastric vessels
Superficial circumflex iliac vessels
Internal pudendal vessels
Ovarian vessels
items.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery and vein run beneath the rectus muscle and can be injured by lateral extension of the fascial incision, causing rectus sheath or retropubic hematoma. The superficial circumflex iliac branches are subcutaneous and minor. Internal pudendal vessels supply the perineum. Ovarian vessels run in the infundibulopelvic ligament and are far from the abdominal wall.
